abstract: Positioning proteins on DNA-functionalized surfaces offers a way to organize catalytic, recognition and signaling activities across materials from synthetic particles to programmable nanostructures. However, site-specific attachment typically requires protein-oligonucleotide conjugation. Here we adapt a small, de novo designed protein that binds a six-base-pair sequence from one duplex face into a genetically encoded surface adapter. We define geometric constraints near blunt ends, hairpin loops and crossover junctions, and identify linker and site-spacing combinations that increase tandem cis-dimer affinity. In synthetic macrophage receptors, these dimers trigger phagocytosis of DNA-coated beads, preserve sensitivity to origami ligand spacing, and remain active after a 24-hour delay when DNA-conjugated receptors decline. We also design trans-dimers bridging neighboring origami helices to dock fluorescent proteins, enzymes, an antibody fragment and SpyCatcher cargo. Together, these design rules and binding modes establish a modular framework for genetically encoded protein-DNA interfacing that should generalize to new de novo binders.
